DESIGN DECISIONS
  ✓ The check-in path must work offline with a local device snapshot and later
    sync, given the venue's unreliable wifi.
      Why          The venue's connectivity is explicitly stated as unusable,
                   and check-in cannot fail at the door.
      Alternative  An online-only check-in relying on live connectivity.
      Tradeoff     Added complexity of local snapshot freshness and sync
                   conflict handling, in exchange for a check-in path that
                   survives the one moment it can't fail.
  ✓ The event is being treated as its own scoped build within a fixed six-week
    deadline.
  Still to decide
    • What exactly defines a guest as 'approved' and where that status
      originates
    • Whether unsigned-contract freelancers are permitted to work the door
    • Who receives and acts on mismatch alerts — event manager, finance, or both
    • Whether this is a one-off build or the first instance of a reusable event
      kit
    • Whether freelancer contracts and rates already live in another system
      requiring integration

CHALLENGES
  ⚑ One word, two different problems
      Premise      The request treats 'mismatch' as a single alert covering both
                   guest approval and freelancer hours-vs-invoice discrepancies.
      Alternative  Event-ops and back-office reconciliation are structurally
                   different builds — different data models, different urgency
                   (real-time at the door vs. post-event for finance), different
                   owners (door staff vs. finance).
      Consequence  Designing one undifferentiated 'mismatch' concept risks a
                   shallow build that satisfies neither: a door alert that's too
                   noisy to act on, and a finance report that still doesn't tie
                   out.
      Recommend    Split into two explicit rule sets and two acceptance criteria
                   before writing any workflow — attendee approval mismatch, and
                   hours/contract/invoice mismatch — each with its own owner and
                   channel.
  ⚑ Clocking freelancer hours is a legal tripwire
      Premise      The build assumes freelancer hours can simply be tracked and
                   reconciled against invoices like a timesheet.
      Alternative  Under French labor law, freelancers who are clocked in/out
                   and monitored like employees are a classic fact pattern for
                   requalification as disguised employment (salariat déguisé) —
                   freelance invoicing is normally tied to a deliverable or
                   mission, not hours worked.
      Consequence  If the app effectively timestamps freelancer
                   arrival/departure and drives invoice amounts from those
                   hours, the client may be building evidence against their own
                   contractor classification.
      Recommend    Check with legal/HR before building an hours-based
                   reconciliation — confirm whether the 'mismatch' should be
                   against mission/deliverable terms in the contract, not
                   clocked hours.
  ⚑ Six weeks, two builds, no rehearsal slack
      Premise      The plan treats offline check-in and freelancer/invoice
                   reconciliation as one project deliverable on the same six-
                   week clock.
      Alternative  The event date can't move, so the check-in path — the one
                   thing that fails visibly in front of the client — should get
                   the depth and rehearsal time, while reconciliation could ship
                   as a clean post-event report rather than a live alert.
      Consequence  Splitting effort evenly across both risks an under-rehearsed
                   door experience, which is the one failure mode with no second
                   chance.
      Recommend    Sequence and scope explicitly: harden and rehearse check-in
                   first; de-scope freelancer reconciliation to a post-event
                   reconciliation report unless real-time alerting is proven
                   necessary.

COMPLEXITY  HIGH
    · offline snapshot + sync with conflict resolution across multiple devices
    · two structurally different rule sets bundled under one 'mismatch' concept
    · unclear integration with an existing contract/invoicing system
    · six-week fixed deadline with no room for schedule slip
  Cost driver   the offline sync/conflict-resolution layer plus reconciling two
                disparate rule sets within a fixed six-week window

MAIN RISKS
  ⚠ No confirmed source of truth for freelancer contracts/rates — could mean
    building contract and invoicing data from scratch instead of integrating
  ⚠ Tracking freelancer hours like a timesheet may create employment-
    misclassification exposure under French labor law
  ⚠ Undefined 'approved' status origin means the approval workflow itself may
    need to be built, not just displayed
  ⚠ Fixed event date leaves no fallback if offline sync or reconciliation logic
    isn't rehearsed and stable in time
  ⚠ Alert recipient and permission split are unresolved — risk of an alert
    nobody is actually responsible for acting on

OPPORTUNITIES
  Medium leverage
    ◆ Model the freelancer hours/contract/invoice reconciliation as an extension
      of the existing Mission-Contract-Invoice relationship rather than a
      bespoke event-specific check, so it can be reused across future freelance
      missions.
        ↳ reaches: Mission, Contract, Invoice
  Future idea
    ◆ Build the offline check-in engine (local snapshot + sync) as a reusable
      pattern for future events rather than a one-off, if the client runs events
      regularly.

RECOMMENDED NEXT STEPS
  1. Split 'mismatch' into two explicit rule sets — guest approval mismatch and
    freelancer hours/contract/invoice mismatch — each with its own owner and
    alert channel, before designing workflow.
  2. Confirm with legal/HR whether freelancer hours can be tracked and billed
    this way without risking employee-misclassification exposure.
  3. Confirm whether an existing contract/invoicing system is the source of
    truth for freelancer contracts and rates, or whether this event app owns
    that data fresh.
  4. Decide and lock the offline architecture (local snapshot + sync + conflict
    rule) for the check-in path first, and rehearse it on real venue hardware
    before touching the reconciliation layer.
